title: What If You Never Blew Your Nose Again?

scenes.text: What if you never blew your nose again? Most of your snot already goes somewhere else.
Your airways make roughly a liter of mucus every day, about half a big soda bottle.
Tiny hairs called cilia beat about ten times a second, sweeping it toward the back of your throat.
There, all day long, you swallow it without noticing. Your stomach neutralizes the trapped germs.
A few days into a cold, it turns yellow or green. That color comes from your own white blood cells.
The twist: one hard blow can shove up to a milliliter of mucus back into your sinuses. Sneezes and coughs can't.

description:
What if you never blew your nose? Your airways make roughly a liter of mucus a day, and cilia beating about 10 to 12 times a second sweep it to the throat, where it is swallowed and the stomach neutralizes trapped bacteria. Yellow and green colors come from white blood cells.
A University of Virginia study found nose blowing reaches about 66 mmHg inside the nose and can push up to 1 mL of thick fluid into the sinuses; sneezing and coughing did not. Not medical advice.
